excerpt: Paano magtanim ng mansanas? Here is how traditional Filipino farmers usually plant mansanas (apple), step by step from getting the field ready to the harvest, with the day of each step and what to change for a higher yield.

heroImage.alt: A farm worker planting in a field

blocks.title: This is the traditional way
blocks.text: This guide shows how traditional farmers usually plant mansanas. Use it as a starting point. For a higher yield, update it: plant certified seed or clean planting material, test your soil, and follow the right spacing and fertilizer.

Apple is rare in the Philippines: there is no traditional apple farming here, only a few growers in cool highlands, best known a farm in Kapatagan, Digos City on the slopes of Mt. Apo, and hobby trees in Baguio and Benguet. This short guide shows how those few growers do it with grafted low chill types and by stripping leaves and bending branches to make the tree flower without a winter.

Before you plant, get the field ready with our [land preparation guide for fruit and plantation trees](/land-preparation/fruit-tree-land-preparation). For more on the crop, read [pagtatanim ng puno](/crops/pagtatanim-ng-puno).
When to plant mansanas

Trees are planted at the start of the rains, about May to July. With no winter, growers make their own seasons: after each harvest they strip the leaves and bend the branches, and the tree flowers again, so some trees give two small crops a year.
What you plant

Grafted trees of low chill apple types, which need little cold, bought from a specialty nursery or grafted on hardy rootstock. Trees from the seeds of store apples grow but rarely bear good fruit, and take many years.
Paano magtanim ng mansanas, step by step
Grafted trees in warm places can set a few fruits within a year, but we count the first real harvest at about 36 months (1,080 days). The crop is ready about 3 years after planting.
Before planting (Bago magtanim)

items.title: 14 days before planting: Pick a cool, sunny, well drained spot
items.text: Choose the coolest high ground you have, in full sun, where water never stands. Dig holes about 50 cm wide and deep and mix the topsoil with rotted manure or compost.

parts.title: Lay out the holes
parts.text: Stake the planting spots about 3 by 3 m apart, wider for big, spreading types.

parts.title: Dig and keep the soils apart
parts.text: Dig each hole about 50 cm square and 60 cm deep, piling the dark topsoil on one side and the paler subsoil on the other. Break up the hard bottom with an iron bar.

parts.title: Mix the subsoil
parts.text: Into the subsoil, mix about 500 g of agricultural lime, chicken manure or compost, about half a kerosene can, and about 500 g of complete fertilizer (14 14 14).

parts.title: Fill the hole in two layers
parts.text: Put the mixed subsoil into the hole first and the topsoil over it, then open a small hole in the middle for the tree. Leave it to settle until planting.

parts.title: Keep the bud union high
parts.text: When you plant, trim off broken roots, bury the tree only as deep as it sat in its bag, and keep the graft joint at least 15 cm above the soil. Crumble fine soil around the roots and tramp it firm so no air pockets stay.

blocks.text: Planting day (Pagtatanim)

items.title: Planting day: Plant at the start of the rains
items.text: Set the grafted tree at the same depth it grew, graft joint above the soil, firm the soil, water and stake it. Growers plant about 3 to 4 m apart. Trials used rows as close as 3 m x 1 m.

blocks.text: Care while it grows (Pag aalaga)

items.title: Day 7: Mulch, water and feed lightly
items.text: Mulch the base, water in dry spells, and give compost or manure with a little complete fertilizer (14 14 14) every few months.

items.title: Month 6: Bend the long branches
items.text: Pull long upright branches down toward level and tie them with string to stakes or the trunk. Bent branches form flower buds instead of only leaves.

parts.title: Choose young branches full of buds
parts.text: Pick branches one to two years old that carry many sleeping buds along their length.

parts.title: Pull them down level
parts.text: Bend each one gently out to the side until it lies flat, at a right angle to the trunk, and tie its tip with straw rope to a peg driven into the ground.

parts.title: Let the spurs form
parts.text: Buds on the upper side of the bent branch push out shoots, and most of them stay short as fruiting spurs. These spurs carry the flowers in the following year.

items.title: Month 12: Strip the leaves to force flowers
items.text: When the leaves are mature and growth stops, pick off the leaves by hand. New leaves and flowers push out in the following weeks. Growers repeat this after each crop, about twice a year.

parts.title: Strip every leaf from the bent branches
parts.text: When growth has stopped and the leaves are mature, pick off all the leaves on the bent branches by hand. In the highlands the trees never get enough cold to wake their buds, and leaf stripping does that job instead.

parts.title: Watch for flowers in three weeks
parts.text: About three weeks after bending and stripping, the flower buds at the branch tips open and new shoots start from the sleeping buds.

parts.title: Repeat on the spurs next year
parts.text: On older trees, strip the old leaves from the spurs after each crop. Their flower buds open two to three weeks later.

items.title: Month 13: Thin and watch the fruit
items.text: Keep one or two fruits per cluster and remove the rest so they size up. Watch for fruit flies and bag young fruits in paper or net bags.

blocks.text: Harvest (Anihan)

items.title: Year 3: Pick colored, firm fruit
items.text: We count the first real crop at about three years. Pick when the fruit has colored, comes off with a gentle lift and twist, and the seeds inside are brown.

blocks.text: Watering mansanas, stage by stage

The few apple trees here, mostly in the highlands and in trial plots, live on rain and get a pail of water in dry spells. Growers plant them on sloping or raised ground so the roots never stand in water. A pail or hose into a ring basin around the tree. Water in the morning.

blocks.title: Never let mansanas go dry at these stages
blocks.text: Flowering to about four weeks after bloom, when fruit set and size are decided. The last two months before picking, when the fruits swell.

blocks.text:
**Without irrigation.** Plant as the rains begin on the coolest, sunniest high ground with fast drainage, and mulch the ring. Most highland trees get by on rain, with a pail of water in dry spells around flowering and fruit growth.

**In the dry season.** Water when the soil a hand deep is dry, most of all from leaf stripping through flowering and fruit growth.

**In the rainy season.** Apples dislike waterlogged roots: plant on slopes or raised ground and never let water stand around the trunk.

items: **Too little water:** Leaves droop and edges brown, few fruits set, and fruits stay small.
**Too much water:** Yellow leaves, poor growth and rotting roots on soggy ground.

blocks.text: To water better for a higher yield: Keep the soil steadily moist from leaf stripping until four weeks after bloom, and again in the last two months before picking.
Spacing, water and fertilizer for mansanas
Spacing
About 3 to 4 m between trees for home and small farm plantings. Trials used close rows of 3 m x 1 m with small, bent trees.
Water
Rain fed, with watering in dry spells. Apples dislike waterlogged roots, so they go on sloping or raised ground.
Fertilizer

Compost and rotted manure, with small amounts of complete fertilizer (14 14 14) every few months. More potash as fruit fills. To read what a bag really gives, see our guide to [fertilizer for this crop](/blog/fertilizer-for-fruit-trees).
Care and harvest
Care while it grows
Branch bending, leaf stripping after each crop to bring on flowers, light pruning to keep the tree small and open, fruit thinning and bagging.
When and how to harvest
Fruit is picked when colored and firm, with brown seeds, a few months after flowering. Crops are small, and most fruit is sold to visitors or eaten at home.
Common mistakes when planting mansanas

items: Planting seeds from store apples and expecting fruit.
Buying high chill types that never flower without a real winter.
Letting branches grow straight up, so the tree makes leaves and no flowers.

blocks.text: How to get a higher yield of mansanas
The traditional way gets a crop, but small changes add up. These are the first things to change, one season at a time.

items: Buy grafted low chill varieties from a nursery you trust.
Plant only on the coolest high ground you have.
Strip leaves and bend branches on a schedule after each crop.
Test the soil and feed by the result. Bag fruit against flies.
